1.title: the oldest hello
1.hook: you've said it after yoga class; the words inside say more than hello
1.carry: the light in me sees the light in you
1.howItsDone: Hindus greet one another with namaste or namaskar, palms pressed together at the chest and the head slightly bowed. The same gesture is made to elders, to guests and before images of the gods.

screen: `DAY ONE.`

segments.voice: Two palms pressed together. It's on your phone's keyboard, between the thumbs-up and the clapping hands. It's how a yoga class ends. It's how a shopkeeper in Chennai greets a customer at the counter, and how a host in New Jersey welcomes a guest through the door. And there's a word that goes with it, a word plenty of people say without a second thought. Namaste. It sounds like a polite hello, and it is one. But it's built out of two older words, and once you hear them, the greeting gets bigger. Today, in a few minutes, you find out what you've been saying.
screen: `TWO PALMS, PRESSED TOGETHER.` → `NAMASTE.` → `MORE THAN HELLO.`

segments.voice: Break the word open. It's Sanskrit, and the dictionary splits it in two. Namas: a bow. Te: to you. Namaste. I bow to you. That's it. That's the whole literal meaning. So the next question is the interesting one. Bow to what, exactly? Not to your clothes, your job title, or how your day is going. The old texts of this tradition keep pointing inward. One of them, the Chandogya Upanishad, talks about a light that shines above the heavens, higher than everything, in the highest world. And then, in the same breath, it says that this light is the very same light that is inside a person. Out there and in here: one light. Put that next to the greeting, and you get today's line. The light in me sees the light in you. That isn't a dictionary translation of namaste. It's a reading of it, and texts like this one are why the reading makes sense. Notice what that reading assumes about a person. It doesn't open by saying: become worthy first, fix yourself, then come back. Its opening move is that the light is already in there. On a bad day, on no sleep, halfway through a long scroll late at night. Already there. In this reading, the work isn't earning it. It's learning to notice it, in yourself and in whoever is standing across from you. Read that way, a plain hello carries all of it.
screen: `NAMAS — A BOW.` · `TE — TO YOU.` · `THE SAME LIGHT, INSIDE A PERSON.` · `ALREADY IN THERE.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT IN ME SEES THE LIGHT IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day one, and it's small on purpose. One breath, with the bell. If you'd like, press your palms together in front of your chest. Breathe in, slowly, all the way. And as you breathe out, let your head tip forward, just a little. A small bow. Say the word inside, if you want: namaste. Not to anyone in particular yet. Just to the fact that someone is in here, breathing, and showed up today.
Namaste. I bow to you. And underneath it: the light in me sees the light in you. A word that was already in the air. Now you know what's inside it. First word on your strand.
screen: `NAMASTE — your 1st word` → clicks onto an empty word-strand.

segments.voice: Your line to carry: the light in me sees the light in you. Try it once today, on a friend, a stranger, or the person who's hard to like. You don't have to say it out loud. Just see somebody that way for a second. That's day one. You showed up. See you tomorrow.

2.title: the sound the universe hums
2.hook: the sound a room makes together; it's three sounds and a silence
2.tomorrow: the thing that's yours to do
2.howItsDone: Hindus chant om at the start of prayers, mantras and readings of scripture, often at the end too, and it is written as a single sacred sign, ॐ, in homes and temples.

screen: `DAY TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, namaste: I bow to you. Your line was the light in me sees the light in you. Did you see anyone that way, even once? It counts either way. Day two.
screen: `NAMASTE ✓` → `DAY 2.`

segments.voice: A room goes quiet. Someone at the front takes a slow breath, and then everyone makes the same long sound together, strangers on their mats, for a few seconds. Om. Then the mats get rolled up and nobody mentions it. Some people feel a little self-conscious making that sound. Fair enough. But the syllable has a whole old text built around it, and that text doesn't treat it as one sound. It hears three sounds inside it, and then a fourth part that isn't a sound at all. You can feel all of it in your own mouth in a single breath. Today, what om is made of.
screen: `A ROOM, ONE SOUND.` → `OM.` → `THREE SOUNDS, AND A FOURTH.`

segments.voice: Say it slowly and feel where it lives. Aaa: the mouth wide open, the sound at the back of the throat. Uuu: the lips round, and the sound moves forward. Mmm: the lips close, and the hum sits in the front of your face. Open, middle, closed. That's why it's sometimes written aum. The text I mentioned is the Mandukya Upanishad. It opens with a big claim: om is all of this. All that was, all that is, all that will be, and whatever lies beyond time too. Then it does something careful. It gives each sound a state of being. A is waking: the world of things you can see and touch. U is dreaming: the inner world, made of the mind. M is deep, dreamless sleep, where everything goes quiet and nothing is wanted. Three sounds, three states a person passes through in an ordinary day. And then the fourth. The Upanishad calls it simply the fourth. It has no sound. It's the silence after the mmm runs out, and the text says that silence is the self, peaceful, where the noise of the world falls away. So om isn't a sign-off. It's a map. Everything you go through in a day, in one breath, and then the quiet under all of it. Om is said at the start of prayers and readings. The Bhagavad Gita says that acts of offering, giving and discipline begin with it. A first sound, before the words.
screen: `A — WAKING.` · `U — DREAMING.` · `M — DEEP SLEEP.` · `THE FOURTH — THE SILENCE.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING, IN ONE BREATH.`

segments.voice: One breath, with the bell. If you're somewhere you can't make a sound, hum it inside; it works the same. Sit up a little. Breathe in, all the way. Now, slowly, let it out as the sound: aaa, uuu, mmm. Let the mmm go until it runs out on its own. And then don't do anything. Just notice the quiet that's left. That's the fourth part.
Om. Three sounds for waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and a silence for the fourth. Everything, in one breath. Second word on your strand, next to namaste.
screen: `OM — your 2nd word` → clicks onto the strand beside namaste.

segments.voice: Your line to carry: one sound, before words. Once today, before you say something that matters, a text, a call, a hard sentence, take one breath first. That's all. Day two.

3.title: the thing that's yours to do
3.hook: a warrior puts down his bow and says he no longer knows what's right
3.carry: do the thing that's yours to do
3.howItsDone: Hindus speak of dharma as right action and the order that holds life together, and also of svadharma, one's own duty in a given place and stage of life; the Bhagavad Gita is read and recited as a guide to it.

screen: `DAY THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, om: three sounds and a silence. Your line was one sound, before words. Did you take that one breath before speaking? Two words on your strand now. Day three.
screen: `NAMASTE · OM` → `DAY 3.`

segments.voice: On a field called Kurukshetra, two armies face each other. Conch shells blast. Banners go up. And a warrior named Arjuna asks his charioteer to drive him out between the lines, so he can see who he's about to fight. He looks across. Grandfathers. Teachers. Uncles, cousins, sons, friends. His own family, standing in both armies, and many of them on the other side. His mouth goes dry, the bow slips from his hand, and he sinks down onto the seat of his chariot. He says he can't do this. His freeze comes on a battlefield. The same kind of freeze can come anywhere: in a hallway, outside a door nobody wants to open. That moment is where the Bhagavad Gita begins. And the word Arjuna reaches for, to say what he's lost, is today's word.
screen: `TWO ARMIES.` → `HIS OWN FAMILY, ACROSS THE FIELD.` → `THE BOW SLIPS.`

segments.voice: Dharma. In English it gets translated as duty, or law, or religion, and each of those catches only a piece. The Sanskrit comes from a root meaning to hold, to support. Dharma is what holds things up. Teachers sometimes put it this way: the dharma of fire is to burn, the dharma of water is to flow. It's what a thing is for, the part it holds in the whole. Now back to the chariot. Arjuna turns to his driver, who is Krishna, and who turns out to be a great deal more than a driver. And Arjuna says, in the second chapter of the Gita, that his mind is confused about dharma. He doesn't know what's right anymore. Then he says something brave: I am your student. Teach me. The rest of the Gita is that teaching, and we'll come back to it on this path. For today, hold one line from the third chapter. Krishna says it's better to do your own dharma, even imperfectly, than someone else's dharma done well. Your own. The Sanskrit is svadharma. So dharma isn't only a rulebook handed down from above. It's also a question you can ask about your own life, today: what is mine to do here? Not what's easiest. Not what someone else should be doing. Mine. Notice that Arjuna isn't lacking information. He knows exactly who's on that field. What he's lost is the thread of what's his to do. That's the thread the Gita hands back.
screen: `DHARMA — WHAT HOLDS THINGS UP.` · `I AM YOUR STUDENT. TEACH ME.` · `YOUR OWN, EVEN IMPERFECTLY.` · then, large: `WHAT IS MINE TO DO HERE?`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first breath, let one small place come to mind where you're a little frozen. Not the biggest thing. A message you haven't answered, a thing you said you'd do. On the second breath, ask it, silently, once: what's mine to do here? On the third, let the question rest. No plan. Just breathe out.
Dharma. From a root meaning to hold. What holds things up, and your own share of the holding. Third word.
screen: `DHARMA — your 3rd word`.

segments.voice: Your line: do the thing that's yours to do. Pick the small frozen one from the practice and do one piece of it today. One reply, one step. That's day three.

4.title: why it's said three times
4.hook: om shanti shanti shanti: three times, never once, and there's a reason
4.tomorrow: why Indian kids touch their grandparents' feet
4.howItsDone: Hindu prayers, readings of the Upanishads and ceremonies often close with om shanti shanti shanti, the word for peace said three times.

screen: `DAY FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, dharma: what holds things up. Your line was do the thing that's yours to do. Did you do one piece of the frozen thing? If not, it's still there, and that's fine. Day four.
screen: `DHARMA — WHAT HOLDS THINGS UP.` → `DAY 4.`

segments.voice: Om shanti shanti shanti. It closes the peace chants that open the Upanishads, and you may have heard it at the end of a class or a ceremony. Count them. Not once. Not twice. Three times. Repeating a word for emphasis is common enough, but there's a more specific answer here. Traditional teachers explain the three shantis as a kind of checklist, a diagnosis of where trouble comes from. And the three make a handy way to sort an ordinary day.
screen: `SHANTI. SHANTI. SHANTI.` → `WHY THREE?` → `A CHECKLIST.`

segments.voice: Shanti means peace. Not the peace of a treaty. The settled kind: calm, quiet, water with nothing stirring it. The Bhagavad Gita asks a blunt question about it. For someone without peace, it says, how can there be happiness? Now, the three. An old philosophical text, the Samkhya Karika, begins by naming suffering of three kinds. And some teachers read the three shantis against that list. Peace from trouble that comes from forces beyond anyone's control, which the old commentators tie to the gods and the elements: storms, floods, the weather, the world. Peace from trouble that comes from other beings: the text that stung, the friend who didn't call, the driver who cut in. And peace from trouble that comes from within: your own body and your own mind. An aching back. The replay that won't switch off. The sentence said years ago that nobody else remembers. The world. Other people. Yourself. Three sources, three shantis. Some teachers who use this list point out something practical. There's only a little anyone can do about the first. There's somewhat more to do about the second. The third is the one most within reach, and it's also the easiest one to skip. So when a prayer or a reading ends this way, it isn't padding. It's going down the list. Peace out there. Peace between us. Peace in here. And then it stops. There's nothing to add after the third one.
screen: `1 — THE WORLD.` · `2 — OTHER PEOPLE.` · `3 — YOUR OWN MIND.` · `THE THIRD IS WITHIN REACH.` · then, large: `THREE SOURCES. THREE PEACES.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell, one shanti on each. First breath out: shanti, toward the world, whatever's on fire out there today. Second breath out: shanti, toward one person you're not at peace with. You don't have to forgive them. Just wish the space between you quieter. Third breath out: shanti, toward your own mind. As kindly as you'd say it to a friend.
Shanti. Peace, the settled kind. Said three times, for three directions: the world, others, and your own mind. Fourth word.
screen: `SHANTI — your 4th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: peace, peace, peace. When something rattles you today, notice which of the three it came from: the world, another person, or your own mind. Just notice. That's day four.

5.title: why Indian kids touch their grandparents' feet
5.hook: a child bends to an elder's feet, and a hand comes down on the child's head
5.carry: bow to what came before you
5.howItsDone: In Hindu families, children and younger adults greet parents, grandparents and teachers with pranam, often bending to touch their feet, and the elder answers with a hand on the head and a blessing.

screen: `DAY FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, shanti, three times over. Your line was peace, peace, peace. When something rattled you, which of the three did it come from: the world, another person, or your own mind? Day five.
screen: `SHANTI · SHANTI · SHANTI` → `DAY 5.`

segments.voice: A grandmother comes through the front door with her bags. Before anyone says hello, a twelve-year-old crosses the room, bends down, and touches her feet. Her hand comes down and rests on the top of the child's head for a second. She says a few words under her breath. Then everybody goes back to arguing about dinner. The whole thing takes two seconds. If you grew up with it, your knees know it without thinking. If you didn't, it can look from the outside like bowing to a boss. Inside the gesture, something else is being said, and it goes in both directions. Today's word is the bow.
screen: `A CHILD BENDS TO THE FEET.` → `A HAND ON THE HEAD.` → `TWO SECONDS. TWO DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: Pranam. It's Sanskrit, built from pra, forward, and nam, to bend or bow. To bend forward: a respectful greeting. You met its cousin on day one. Namaste and pranam share that same bowing root. Touching the feet has its own name, charan sparsh. Charan, the feet. Sparsh, a touch. Here's one way it's explained. The head is the high point of a person, where the pride sits, and the opinions. The feet are the low point, and they've walked further down the road than yours have. So when the high point of you meets the low point of them, the gesture says something like: you've been where I'm going. Thank you. Now watch the other half. The elder doesn't just receive it. A hand comes down onto the head. That's a blessing, an ashirvad, given back. Respect is given. A blessing comes back. Nobody walks away smaller. An old law book, the Manusmriti, puts a promise on this habit. For the one who greets and serves elders, it says, four things grow: length of life, learning, good name and strength. Some read that as a promise, some as a description of what the habit does to a person. Either way, the gesture says one plain thing: nobody invents themselves. Somebody walked ahead, did hard things, and passed the road down. Pranam is a two-second way of saying so.
screen: `PRA + NAM — TO BEND FORWARD.` · `HIGH POINT MEETS LOW POINT.` · `RESPECT GIVEN, BLESSING BACK.` · `FOUR THINGS GROW.` · then, large: `YOU'VE BEEN WHERE I'M GOING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who came before you. A grandparent, a teacher, anyone who made your road easier, living or not. Let their face come clear. Then, with the bell, breathe in, and as you breathe out, bow to them in your mind. Or tip your head a little, for real. Stay bowed for one more breath, and picture the hand coming back, resting on your head. Whatever they'd have said, let them say it.
Pranam. To bend forward. A bow to the ones who walked first, and a blessing that comes back. Fifth word.
screen: `PRANAM — your 5th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bow to what came before you. Today, thank one older person for one specific thing they did. A text is fine. That's day five.

6.title: the one at every doorway
6.hook: an elephant-headed figure on the dashboard, by the door, at the top of the page
6.howItsDone: Hindus honor Ganesha first at ceremonies, weddings and new beginnings, keep his image near doorways and in shops, and some write shri ganeshaya namah at the top of a page before starting to write.

screen: `DAY SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, pranam: the bow, and the blessing that comes back. Your line was bow to what came before you. Did you thank someone? Today you meet someone. Day six.
screen: `PRANAM — RESPECT GIVEN, BLESSING BACK.` → `DAY 6.`

segments.voice: A small statue glued to a taxi dashboard, nodding over every pothole. A picture above a shop counter. A carved figure beside a front door. On a wedding invitation, sometimes just his name, printed at the very top before anyone else's. Elephant head. Round belly. One tusk whole, one broken. He sits where things start: doorways, first pages, first days. His name is Ganesha. To someone meeting him for the first time, an elephant-headed god can look strange. Give it a few minutes, and he turns out to stand for something easy to want at the start of anything hard. Someone to clear the road.
screen: `THE DASHBOARD. THE DOOR. THE FIRST PAGE.` → `ELEPHANT HEAD, ONE TUSK.` → `WHERE THINGS START.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. Ganesha is gana plus isha: lord of the ganas, the attendants of the god Shiva. He has another name too, Ganapati, which means much the same thing. But the title that explains the doorway is this one: Vighnaharta. Vighna is an obstacle. Harta is one who removes. The remover of obstacles. That's why he's honored first. Before a ceremony, before a wedding, before a new shop opens its shutters or a student sits down to an exam, Ganesha is invoked at the start. Some people write a short line at the top of a page before they begin: shri ganeshaya namah. Listen to that last word. Namah. It's the same bow you learned on day one, in namaste. A bow to Ganesha, before the work. How he got the elephant's head is a story, and a good one, and you'll hear it later on this path. Today, just look at him. There's a popular way of reading his body. Big ears: listen more than you talk. Small eyes: focus. Big belly: take in whatever life serves you, the good and the hard. And the broken tusk. Tradition says Ganesha wrote down the Mahabharata as the sage Vyasa spoke it, and one story people tell says that when his pen gave out, he snapped off his own tusk and kept writing. In the Puranas he is also a guardian of thresholds, and the same lord who removes obstacles can place them too. At a doorway, people ask him for the first: a clear way in.
screen: `GANESHA — LORD OF THE GANAS.` · `VIGHNAHARTA — REMOVER OF OBSTACLES.` · `HONORED FIRST, BEFORE THE WORK.` · `BIG EARS, SMALL EYES, ONE TUSK.` · then, large: `CLEAR THE ROAD, THEN BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Find something near you that marks a start: a door, a laptop lid, the cover of a notebook. Rest a hand on it. Let one thing you're about to begin this week come to mind. With the bell, name what's in the way, quietly, just once: fear, time, a person, an excuse. Then ask for the road to be clear, in whatever way fits you. Some who pray begin with his name: shri ganeshaya namah. Or just picture the road, open. Breathe out, and lift your hand.
Ganesha. Lord of the ganas, remover of obstacles, the one at the door. Sixth word, and the first name on your strand.
screen: `GANESHA — your 6th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: clear the road, then begin. Today, before the next thing you start, take one second and name what's in the way. Then begin. That's day six.

7.title: a handrail made of sound
7.hook: your mind already loops a phrase all day; a mantra is choosing which one
7.tomorrow: what your grandmother was actually doing
7.howItsDone: Hindus repeat mantras aloud, in a whisper or silently, sometimes counting them on a string of prayer beads called a mala; this repetition is called japa, and the Gayatri mantra is recited at dawn and dusk by some families.

screen: `DAY SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesha, the remover of obstacles. Your line was clear the road, then begin. Did you name what was in the way? And look back: namaste, om, dharma, shanti, pranam, Ganesha. Six words. Day seven.
screen: `NAMASTE · OM · DHARMA · SHANTI · PRANAM · GANESHA` → `DAY 7.`

segments.voice: Nine in the morning, a song from the grocery store slips into someone's head, and it's still looping at lunch. Or it isn't a song. It's a sentence from last night's argument, or a worry about money, going around and around on its own. Nobody chose it. The mind grabbed a phrase and kept playing it. That isn't a personal flaw. Minds do that. The practice of mantra meets that habit with a practical question instead of a fight. If the mind is going to repeat something anyway, what if you picked what it repeats?
screen: `A PHRASE ON A LOOP.` → `NOBODY CHOSE IT.` → `WHAT IF YOU PICKED IT?`

segments.voice: Mantra. The Sanskrit dictionary takes it from man, to think, with tra, an instrument. An instrument of thought. A tool for the mind. And a traditional explanation hears a second meaning: the tra of protection, so a mantra is what protects the mind that dwells on it. You've already met a few. Om, from day two. Om shanti shanti shanti, from day four. Shri ganeshaya namah, from yesterday. There are many more. One is a single verse of the Rig Veda, the Gayatri mantra. In it, the one praying meditates on the bright, worthy light of the god Savitar, the sun as the power that rouses and sets things moving, and asks that he stir and guide our thoughts. A prayer about thinking, said to train the thinking. The Bhagavad Gita gives repetition a place of honor. In the tenth chapter, Krishna lists the forms in which he can be found, and among offerings, he says, he is japa: the quiet repetition of a mantra. Here's how it works in practice. The mind can only hold so much at once. If it's holding the mantra, there's less room for the replay. It's less like a spell and more like a handrail. On a dark staircase, you don't stop to study the dark. You put your hand on the rail and keep going. When the loop comes back, you don't argue with it. You go back to the rail. That's the whole move. Six days ago the strand started with namaste. Now there are seven words on it, and three things you've said along the way, om, the shantis and the line to Ganesha, turn out to have been mantras all along.
screen: `MAN — TO THINK. TRA — A TOOL.` · `OM, SHANTI, THE GAYATRI.` · `AMONG OFFERINGS, I AM JAPA.` · `THE LOOP COMES BACK. SO DO YOU.` · then, large: `A HANDRAIL MADE OF SOUND.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell, with the mantra you already know. Breathe in. On the way out, say om, silently, just in the mind. Again: in, and om. If something else drifts in, a song, a list, a worry, don't push it away. Just put your hand back on the rail. Third breath. In. Om. And notice whether it gave you somewhere to go.
Mantra. An instrument of thought, a tool for the mind, repeated on purpose. Seventh word. A week's worth.
screen: `MANTRA — your 7th word` → the strand, seven lit → `WEEK ONE. DONE.`

segments.voice: Your line: a handrail made of sound. Today, once, when the replay starts, put your hand on the rail. Om, three times, silently. See what happens. That's week one: seven words, and what's inside each one. Tomorrow, the flower, the flame and the bell. Day seven.

screen: `DAY 7 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT YOUR GRANDMOTHER WAS ACTUALLY DOING.`
